title: Thermal ordering under Markovian relaxation: a finite-time criterion and its limits
shortTitle: When a hotter system can never relax faster
oneLine: A simple cone test rules out Mpemba-type crossings at every time; for bosonic baths with common coupling it holds exactly when the emission weight is concave, so Ohmic and Drude–Lorentz baths pass and super-Ohmic baths can produce a certified crossing.
abstract: When a hotter and a cooler copy of a system relax in the same bath, the Markovian Mpemba effect is a crossing of their distances from equilibrium. This candidate gives a sufficient test that rules out such crossings at every time: if a Markov operator and its equilibrium adjoint preserve the cone of observables with nondecreasing arithmetic prefix means, cooling Gibbs preparations stay ordered for relative entropy in both orientations, squared Hellinger distance and Rényi divergences of order 0<α≤2, including for common schedules of noncommuting stages. For complete-graph bosonic population rates with common pair coupling, the test holds for every spectrum and every bath temperature exactly when the spontaneous jump weight is concave. Ohmic weights with cutoff at least half the spectral width, Drude–Lorentz weights below √3 times their cutoff and sub-Ohmic power laws qualify; super-Ohmic weights never do, and for the cube law on four levels an actual relative-entropy crossing is certified by exact interval arithmetic. The limits are mapped: an exact five-state cone-preserving example has a brief total-variation reversal, and for every N≥4 there are N-level systems with a slow-mode inversion although no proper induced subsystem shows one. The closest antecedent already excludes the slow-mode effect for Ohmic and sub-Ohmic spectra; the increment is all-time ordering at every bath temperature with an exact necessity direction. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: All-time ordering test (Theorem 2, proof): if a likelihood-ratio Markov operator K and its π-adjoint preserve the prefix-mean cone, cooling Gibbs preparations stay ordered at every time in both relative entropies, squared Hellinger distance and Rényi divergences of order 0<α≤2; heating uses the convex class; common schedules of noncommuting stages are covered (Corollary 3).

Exact physical class (Theorem 4, proof): for complete-graph bosonic population rates with common coupling, cone preservation holds for every spectrum of width at most D and every bath temperature if and only if the jump weight J is concave on [0, D]; necessity needs all level counts and arbitrarily cold baths jointly.
Standard baths (Proposition 6, proof): d^s is concave iff 0≤s≤1; d^s e^(−d/ω_c) iff 0<s≤1 and D≤(s+√s)ω_c (Ohmic: D≤2ω_c); Drude–Lorentz iff D≤√3 ω_c; super-Ohmic weights never.

Certified super-Ohmic crossing (Proposition 8, exact certificate): J=d³ on levels 0,1,2,3 with e^(−β_b)=2/3 breaks the cone, and the relative entropies of two cooling preparations cross between t=1/5 and t=3/10.

Total variation is a genuine exception (Proposition 9, exact certificate): a five-state cone-preserving reversible generator has certified heating total-variation crossings in (10.46, 10.47) and (10.47, 10.48), an effect of about 10⁻⁴ relative.

No local certificate (Theorem 10, proof; Remark 11, certificate): for every N≥4 an N-level finite-bath system has a slow-mode inversion and total-variation crossing although every proper induced subsystem excludes slow-mode inversion; the finite-bath threshold is existential.

narration: When can a hotter object never cool faster? An Evidence Press briefing. Put two copies of the same small system, one hotter and one cooler, in contact with the same cold surroundings. You would expect the hotter copy to stay farther from equilibrium all the way down. Sometimes it does not: the two relaxation curves cross, and the hotter copy arrives first. This is called the Markovian Mpemba effect, after the old puzzle about hot water freezing faster. This release asks when such crossings can be ruled out at every moment, without solving the dynamics. It gives a simple test. If the dynamics, and its time reverse, keep a certain family of increasing-on-average quantities increasing on average, then the two copies stay in order at all times, for several standard measures of distance from equilibrium. For a standard model of quantum levels coupled to a bath of oscillators, the test passes for every energy spectrum and every bath temperature exactly when the bath's emission strength bends downwards with frequency. Ohmic baths with a high enough cutoff, Drude-Lorentz baths and sub-Ohmic baths pass. Super-Ohmic baths, such as three-dimensional phonons, fail, and for one such bath the paper certifies a real crossing using exact interval arithmetic. The guarantee has limits: total variation distance can still reverse briefly, and checking small subsystems cannot certify a large system. An earlier paper already excluded the slow-mode version of the effect for similar baths; the new contribution is all-time ordering with an exact boundary. The results have written proofs and exact computer checks. This is an anonymous, AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate, not peer reviewed or independently reproduced. Published on 28 October 2026, its paper and evidence are linked from the Evidence Press release page. This briefing uses an AI-generated voice and is not additional scientific evidence.

decisionObject.description: A two-adjoint prefix-mean cone criterion orders cooling Gibbs preparations at all times for a divergence family; for complete-graph bosonic rates with common coupling, cone preservation for all spectra and bath temperatures is equivalent to concavity of the jump weight; certified boundary examples for super-Ohmic baths, total variation and induced subsystems.
decisionObject.scope: Finite classical Markov population dynamics with one bath; complete transition graph and common pair coupling for the physical class; Gibbs preparations on one side of the bath. Sparse graphs, arbitrary couplings and quantum coherences are not addressed.

semanticBridge.description: Section 4.5 states the rate convention J=2π|g|²𝒥 and translates Eq. (5) of Avitan et al. (arXiv v1): their exponent s equals the power-law exponent of J plus one, so their Ohmic case is not concave and the cube-law example lies outside their exclusion range.
